name: .eu Top-Level Domain Regulation
evidence_rating: thin: registry statistics only; no evaluation of the new Regulation yet (due 2027); no independent studies
summary: The Regulation modernised the rules for the .eu internet domain and opened it to EU citizens living anywhere. Registrations have been broadly flat since it was proposed, at about 3.7-3.8 million (end-2025). The new framework has applied only since October 2022 and its first evaluation is due by 2027; no independent study exists.

indicators.objective: The proposal's financial statement has no indicators section (1.4.4 is about synergies); the Commission must assess the .eu domain five years after application (i.e. by October 2027) and every three years after

indicators.indicator: Promote the attractiveness and uptake of .eu (incl. opening eligibility to EU citizens living outside the EU)
indicators.evidence: Registrations broadly flat: 3.7m in April 2021 and about 3.79m at end-2025 (EURid figures); Brexit losses offset by pandemic demand; Q3 2025 was the strongest growth quarter.

indicators.indicator: Governance reflecting best practice and EU public interest (multistakeholder council)
indicators.evidence: Multistakeholder Council and new registry selection set up under the Regulation (applies since 13 Oct 2022); no assessment of effects yet.
Registry reports 100% availability, abuse-prevention early warning system and know-your-customer checks (2019-2021).

literature.citation: European Commission (2018), Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal on the implementation and functioning of the .eu top-level domain (executive summary SWD(2018) 121), SWD(2018) 120
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal on the implementation and functioning of the .eu top-level domain (executive summary SWD(2018) 121)
literature.headline: Preferred option: principles-based framework, separate multistakeholder advisory body, relaxed eligibility (EU citizenship criterion) and direct registration; no quantified targets
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected simpler, more flexible rules and wider eligibility to make the .eu domain more attractive, without setting numerical targets.

literature.citation: European Commission (2018), REFIT evaluation of Regulations 733/2002 and 874/2004 on the .eu top-level domain (executive summary), SWD(2018) 122
literature.title: REFIT evaluation of Regulations 733/2002 and 874/2004 on the .eu top-level domain (executive summary)
literature.headline: Old framework still delivered its benefits but was outdated and rigid, with governance and accountability deficiencies and poor fit with a fast-changing domain market
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's evaluation of the old .eu rules found them still useful but outdated and too rigid.

literature.citation: European Commission (2022), Report on the implementation, functioning and effectiveness of the .eu Top-Level Domain from April 2019 to April 2021, COM(2022) 1
literature.title: Report on the implementation, functioning and effectiveness of the .eu Top-Level Domain from April 2019 to April 2021
literature.headline: 3.7 million .eu domains in April 2021 (8th largest ccTLD); growth flattened as Brexit losses were offset by pandemic demand; citizens abroad allowed to register; 100% availability
literature.summary_plain: In 2021 the .eu domain had 3.7 million registrations and growth had flattened.
literature.period_geography: EU, 2019-2021 (mostly before the new Regulation applied)

literature.citation: EURid (registry) (2026), Q4 2025 quarterly update, EURid quarterly report
literature.title: Q4 2025 quarterly update
literature.headline: 3,790,453 .eu registrations at end-2025; 193,047 new registrations in Q4 2025
literature.summary_plain: By end-2025 the .eu domain had about 3.79 million registrations, roughly the same as in 2021.
literature.interested_party: EURid is the registry operator under contract with the Commission
